You are an independent adversarial reviewer for a draft root README. Read it at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/bdff267d-67dc-5bb9-b970-8c3dfaa634b6/scratchpad/fortress-readme.md. The repository is /home/user/fortress — a revival of Sun/Oracle's Fortress language (Guy Steele, 2003–2012), full historical git history carried forward to a modern Java toolchain. You may read files in the repo to verify factual claims (paths, file counts, names), but your job is the README text, not the codebase.

Review it through the CURATOR'S LENS the repository owner has articulated. His standards, in essence:

1. **This is a museum exhibit, not an active project.** The README is an exhibition catalog: what Fortress is, how it came about, what research it produced — and only at the end, for the intrigued visitor, how to run it. Anything that reads like a modern OSS project pitching for adoption ("quickstart", badges, bragging about test counts, "getting started" vocabulary of the latest JavaScript framework) is wrong in kind.
2. **Humble custodianship, zero self-credit.** The revival/modernization work must appear only as a terse, anonymous, factual note. The original authors are the story. Any sentence where the curators pat themselves on the back — even faintly ("fully green", "healthier than", achievement framing) — must be flagged. Attribution lives in commit messages, not the README.
3. **Timeless formulation.** No numbers, timings, or state that will rot (test counts, build seconds, "current rung", "2026", counts of commits). Flag every time-bound or mission-specific detail. Dates that are historical facts (2007, 2012) are fine.
4. **No meta commentary.** The document should never narrate itself ("in the order a new reader needs it", "see below") or the drafting process.
5. **Factual precision with primary-source humility.** Flag any claim that is asserted more confidently than the evidence in the repo supports, any claim a reader could falsify, and any inconsistency between sections.

Also review as a fresh outside reader: Is the structure (intro → History → The research → Repository tour → Building, walking and running → Lineage and license) coherent? Does anything repeat? Is any sentence confusing without context the reader lacks? Are the links plausible (spot-check a few paths exist in the repo)? Is the tone even throughout — does any section drift back into promotional or blog register? Is anything important about the exhibit MISSING that a museum catalog would include?

Be adversarial: hunt for violations of the five standards above, awkward phrasing, over-claiming, under-explaining, and structural weaknesses. Do NOT rewrite the document. Produce a numbered list of concrete findings, each with: the quoted offending text (short), why it fails (which standard or reader problem), and a suggested minimal fix. Order by severity. Include a short closing paragraph on overall fitness. Your final message text is the deliverable — plain markdown, no preamble.

You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.

Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. 1	# Fortress
2	
3	Fortress was Sun Microsystems' experimental programming language for
4	high-performance computation, designed at Sun Labs under **Guy L. Steele Jr.**
5	and developed from 2003 to 2012. Steele's ambition, as quoted in the 2005
6	announcement coverage, was to do *"for Fortran what Java did for C"*; the
7	project's own tagline was simpler — **"Simple parallelism, beautiful code."**
8	In practice it became something broader — a laboratory for
9	programming-language ideas that are still being absorbed by mainstream
10	languages today:
11	
12	- **A growable language.** Following Steele's "Growing a Language" (OOPSLA
13	  1998), almost everything — operators, loops, even the parallel machinery of
14	  `∑` and friends — is defined in libraries, not the compiler.
15	- **A mathematical language.** Syntax modeled on whiteboard mathematics:
16	  Unicode operators (`∈`, `⊆`, `⌊x⌋`, `∑`), juxtaposition as a user-definable
17	  operator (`3 sin pi x`), nontransitive operator precedence (`a+b ∨ c+d` is
18	  rejected rather than misparsed), and comments that render as wiki markup.
19	- **A parallel language.** Loops, tuples, argument evaluation, and big
20	  reduction operators are implicitly parallel; a work-stealing runtime
21	  balances the load ("do for processors what GC does for memory"); `atomic`
22	  blocks are backed by transactional memory.
23	- **Traits, multiple inheritance, and symmetric multimethod dispatch**, with
24	  overloading checked by the Meet Rule — plus algebraic traits (`Monoid`,
25	  `Ring`, …) and design-by-contract woven into the type system.
26	
27	This repository preserves that codebase: the complete surviving history,
28	January 2007 through August 2012, carried forward so that it still builds
29	and runs on today's Java platform.
30	
31	## History
32	
33	**2003–2006: DARPA HPCS.** Steele started the project in 2003 as Sun's
34	language effort within DARPA's High Productivity Computing Systems program.
35	When DARPA narrowed HPCS funding in late 2006, Sun continued Fortress as a
36	research project.
37	
38	**2007–2008: open source and Fortress 1.0.** The code was opened in January
39	2007 (this repository's history begins 2007-01-04). The 1.0 specification
40	and the reference interpreter followed in 2008.
41	
42	**2008–2012: the type-system frontier.** Work shifted from the interpreter
43	to compiling Fortress to the JVM, and to the hard theory: the Meet Rule,
44	the return type rule, and run-time instantiation of generics. In his 2016
45	JuliaCon retrospective, Steele was frank about where it stalled: solving
46	type constraints at run time was "non-trivial — a euphemism for exponential
47	cost." *"So we had a grand vision, but could not quite pull it off."* The
48	final commits in this history, from August 2012, are exactly that work.
49	
50	**2012: wind-down.** Oracle Labs concluded the project in the summer of
51	2012 — Steele's announcement, [*Fortress Wrapping Up*](https://web.archive.org/web/20121007034544/https://blogs.oracle.com/projectfortress/entry/fortress_wrapping_up)
52	(July 20, 2012), survives in the Wayback Machine. His 2016 retrospective
53	lists what they consider proven and worth reusing: symmetric multimethod
54	dispatch with generics, work-stealing implicit parallelism,
55	generator/reducer-factored collections, mathematical syntax that both
56	parses and pretty-prints, nontransitive precedence, and physical dimensions
57	and units in the type system. Ideas seeded here have since surfaced
58	elsewhere — Steele points to Swift's optional binding (`if let`) as a
59	direct descendant of Fortress's `if x <- z then … end`.
60	
61	Retrospective sources: Guy L. Steele Jr., *Fortress Features and Lessons
62	Learned*, JuliaCon 2016 — [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EZD3Scuv02g);
63	notes in [`research/extracts/`](research/extracts/SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md).
64	
65	## The research
66	
67	Fortress produced a substantial body of programming-language research. The
68	sources of the specification and of several papers live in this repository.
69	
70	### The language specification
71	
72	- [`Specification-1.0-frozen/`](Specification-1.0-frozen/) — the frozen
73	  **Fortress 1.0 specification** (March 2008), with the rendered
74	  [`fortress.1.0.pdf`](Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf).
75	- [`Specification/`](Specification/) — the post-1.0 evolving specification
76	  LaTeX, richer in places than any published PDF.
77	- [`Documentation/Specification/`](Documentation/Specification/) — a later,
78	  partial restart of the specification effort.
79	
80	### Papers with sources in this repo
81	
82	- [`Papers/Types/`](Papers/Types/) — *Type Checking Modular Multiple
83	  Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance*
84	  (Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, Steele — **OOPSLA
85	  2011**), with a journal draft on the return type rule in
86	  [`journal/`](Papers/Types/journal/).
87	- [`Papers/Dispatch/`](Papers/Dispatch/) — *Implementing Fully Modular,
88	  Statically Typed, Symmetric Multimethod Dispatch* (Steele, Chase, et al.),
89	  a POPL 2011 submission draft, with a
90	  [rendered PDF](Papers/Dispatch/SteelePOPL2011.pdf).
91	- [`Papers/Welterweight/`](Papers/Welterweight/) — *Dynamic Dispatch and
92	  Type Inference Semipredicates* ("Welterweight Fortress"; Chase, Hilburn,
93	  Luchangco, et al.), an unpublished draft.
94	- [`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/`](Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/) —
95	  *Enforcing Fortress' Return Type Rule at Runtime*, a draft with working
96	  notes.
97	- [`Papers/Implementation/`](Papers/Implementation/) — implementation
98	  notes: *Fortress function and method encodings* and *Mapping Fortress
99	  type relationships onto the JVM type system*, with a
100	  [rendered PDF](Papers/Implementation/FortressEncodings-rendered.pdf).
101	
102	The unpublished drafts — the return-type-rule journal work, Welterweight,
103	and the runtime and implementation notes — are the written record of the
104	problem that ultimately stopped the project: making generic methods,
105	multiple inheritance, and fully symmetric dispatch coexist soundly requires
106	solving systems of type constraints at run time. That work's one public
107	afterlife is a family of Oracle patents on the dispatch machinery
108	([US 8,843,887](https://patents.google.com/patent/US8843887B2/en) and
109	siblings), filed days after the final commits here.
110	
111	Related published work by the team (sources not in this repo) includes
112	*Object-Oriented Units of Measurement* (OOPSLA 2004), *Growing a Syntax*
113	(FOOL 2009), and Steele's ICFP 2009 talk *Organizing Functional Code for
114	Parallel Execution; or, foldl and foldr Considered Slightly Harmful* — the
115	generators-and-reducers story. A curated index of talks, decks, and recovery
116	provenance is in [`research/README.md`](research/README.md).
117	
118	## Repository tour
119	
120	The top level:
121	
122	- [`ProjectFortress/`](ProjectFortress/) — the toolchain: all Java/Scala
123	  source under `src/com/sun/fortress/`, ~1,800 `.fss` test programs, and
124	  vendored third-party jars. Built by the root [`build.xml`](build.xml)
125	  (the one inside `ProjectFortress/` is a deprecation stub).
126	- [`Library/`](Library/) — the standard library: 53 components as
127	  `.fss`/`.fsi` pairs; `FortressLibrary.fss` is the 4,518-line prelude.
128	  Top-level [`CompilerLibrary/`](CompilerLibrary/) holds API stubs for the
129	  compiler path.
130	- [`bin/`](bin/) — the `fortress` launcher and 34 supporting scripts.
131	- [`Specification/`](Specification/), [`Papers/`](Papers/),
132	  [`Documentation/`](Documentation/) — the research record (see above), plus
133	  [`Fortify/`](Fortify/), the Emacs-based renderer that typesets Fortress
134	  source as LaTeX math for those documents.
135	- [`explorations/`](explorations/), [`research/`](research/) — revival-era:
136	  verified experiments, the modernization plan, repo internals, and the
137	  Steele research corpus (links and working notes only; copyrighted PDFs are
138	  never committed).
139	- Everything else is the historical artifact being preserved — Sun-era IDE
140	  configs, scratch directories, SVN-metrics scripts — treat with care.
141	  [`README.txt`](README.txt) is Sun's original SVN-era repository guide.
142	
143	Inside `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`, the shape of the
144	implementation:
145	
146	- `Shell.java` — the CLI entry point, dispatching `walk` (interpret),
147	  `compile`, `run`, `parse`, `typecheck`, and friends.
148	- `parser/` — four Rats!-generated packrat parsers (the main grammar plus a
149	  preparser, template parser, and import collector; the generated
150	  `Fortress.java` alone is 2 MB), with hand-written precedence and layout
151	  support in `parser_util/` and the extensible-syntax machinery in
152	  `syntax_abstractions/`.
153	- `nodes/` — 1,071 generated AST classes, produced (along with Scala and
154	  Fortress mirrors of the AST) from the 2,125-line
155	  `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. Generated code is committed;
156	  `ant makeAST` regenerates.
157	- `scala_src/` — the type checker, rewritten in Scala starting February 2009
158	  (remains of the older Java checker sit in `compiler/typechecker/`).
159	- `compiler/` — disambiguation, desugaring, and the JVM bytecode backend
160	  (`codegen/`, `asmbytecodeoptimizer/`); its `WellKnownNames.java` is the
161	  switch that gives the interpreter and compiler paths their different
162	  preludes.
163	- `interpreter/` — the tree-walking reference evaluator, with native
164	  primitives in `glue/`.
165	- `runtimeSystem/` — the work-stealing runtime, and the class-load-time
166	  instantiation of generics that compiled code links against.
167	
168	The full, measured map — every package with file counts and roles, the
169	test-corpora inventory, cache anatomy, and the traps — is in
170	[`explorations/repo-internals.md`](explorations/repo-internals.md).
171	
172	## Building, walking and running
173	
174	Fortress needs only a JDK and Apache Ant. The 2012 toolchain has been
175	modernized in small, individually tested steps — a ladder from JDK 8 up to
176	current JDKs, each rung gated on the complete original test suite and
177	tagged, so you can check out whichever era of the Java ecosystem you want
178	to explore.
179	
180	```bash
181	export JAVA_HOME=/path/to/jdk
182	export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH
183	export FORTRESS_HOME=$(pwd)                    # repo root
184	ant compileAll
185	./bin/fortress ProjectFortress/demos/buffons.fss
186	```
187	
188	That last command *walks* — the interpreter's own term for direct
189	evaluation — one of the original Sun Labs demos: Buffon's needle,
190	estimating π by dropping needles in parallel.
191	
192	There is also a partial JVM bytecode compiler (`fortress compile`, then
193	`fortress run`); it is incomplete — some constructs were never implemented
194	— but what exists works. The interpreter requires the filename (without
195	`.fss`) to match the component name, and the compiler path needs imported
196	library components compiled into its cache first — recipe, traps, and
197	troubleshooting in
198	[`explorations/repo-internals.md`](explorations/repo-internals.md).
199	
200	To run the test suite: `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`.
201	
202	## Lineage and license
203	
204	This repository carries the full available git history of the original
205	`projectfortress.sun.com` Subversion repository, from the January 2007
206	opening to the August 2012 wind-down, together with the later migration
207	work that keeps it running — see the commit history for lineage and
208	attribution.
209	
210	Fortress is BSD-licensed — see [`LICENSE`](LICENSE).
211

explorations/swift-vs-fortress-explainer.md:88:Two nested comprehensions: `BIG ||` concatenates a row of characters, `BIG //` joins rows with newlines. No loop, no mutation, no index arithmetic beyond the coordinate formula — and no requested parallelism, because none needs requesting. Fortress evaluates comprehensions as *reductions over a monoid*: string concatenation is associative, so the runtime is free to split the range, render chunks on different threads via work-stealing, and combine. The slide-deck slogan: reduction operators and comprehensions "are exactly like" each other — `∑` desugars to a generator call with a `SumReduction` object whose entire definition is `empty()` and `join(a,b) = a + b`. Declare the algebraic structure; the evaluation strategy follows.

input.description: Read Steele extract around quotes and Swift claim

content.content:
- Slide 42 — Run-time type inference: `crunch(myList)` where
  `myList: List[\Object\] =` a list of threads must infer `T = Thread` at run
  time.
- Slide 43 — Static parameters with interdependent bounds:
  `mangle[\M extends {PartialOrder[\M\], Group[\M,+\]}, F extends M->N,
  N extends List[\M\]\](x:M, f:F): N` — "In general, this requires solving a
  system of type inequalities at run time."
- Slide 44 — **Where We Got Stuck**: generic methods × symmetry requirement →
  parametric meet rule and return type rule → nontrivial run-time constraint
  solving — "'Non-trivial' is a euphemism for 'exponential cost'";
  "Contravariance and union types interact badly"; mitigated by imposing a
  lexical asymmetry on method type parameters; "another nasty case popped up:
  the return type rule has nontrivial consequences." **"So we had a grand
  vision, but could not quite pull it off."**
  **[repo]** This is precisely the subject of the trunk's final commits —
  karl.naden's `Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/` (incl. "rtr algorithm",
  "using constraints", RTRinstantionTheory.tex) and
  `Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`, preserved in the graft.

## 45–49. Lessons and reflections

- Slide 45 — **We learned some good things**: generic types with multiple
  inheritance of generic methods and symmetric dispatch; parallelism with
  automatic work-stealing; factoring parallelism on collections via generators
  and reducers; parsing AND pretty-printing mathematical syntax; nontransitive
  precedence; physical dimensions/units inside a generic type system. "My
  current thinking is to back off and try to exploit a subset of these ideas
  using a less complex type system."
- Slide 46 — Syntax tradeoffs: math notation designed for concision, not
  robustness; juxtaposition made programmable — "sometimes this worked
  beautifully, sometimes it required some weird contortions"; Haskell and Scala
  each capture a PART of mathematical tradition more consistently.
- Slide 47 — Reflections: **"I knew when I started the Fortress project in
  2003..."** (confirms the 2003 start; git history begins 2007-01-04,
  mid-project). Long shot vs Fortran/Java; "we are too often fearful of
  correcting mistakes"; JavaScript aside ("maybe Worse Is Better").
- Slide 48 — Language life cycles: good ideas survive by hopping between
  languages; "the language that develops an idea may not be the one that
  survives"; "I believe in studying history." Fortress → **Swift optional
  binding**: `if x <- z then f(x) else y end` where `z: Maybe[\T\]`.
- Slide 49 — Closer: Greenspun's Tenth Rule.

work-stealing`. Started March 2011, owned by dr2chase (David Chase), BSD,

The famous "do for Fortran what Java did for C" line does **not** appear
on the archived project pages themselves — it is attested in press
coverage (e.g. HPCwire, JavaOne 2008 reports), so cite it as Sun press
framing, not as the site's own words.
